1.	What dollar losses has the CBC experienced in terms of work done for programs subsequently cancelled or postponed as a result of the strike of CBC technicians?
2.	Were any contracts for advertising cancelled on CBC radio or television as a result of the strike of CBC technicians and, if so (a) how many (b) what was their dollar value?

I am
informed by the CBC as follows: 1. It is not possible to make an accurate calculation as to the dollar value of work done on programs and subsequently lost because of cancellations or postponements due to the technicians' strike. Programs which have to be postponed for showing at a later date are held in inventory and when later shown represent no loss of production costs, although there may be revenue loss or gain from advertising depending on the nature of the program and the time of showing. Programs which have to be cancelled (because work on them has been interrupted and they cannot be completed), or which, if completed, cannot be shown at a later date because they become out-dated, represent a dollar loss which is difficult to calculate accurately. In some cases the expenditure on an uncompleted program is actually less than the expenditure which was budgeted for that program and an actual saving results even when the cost of the cheaper replacement program is taken into account.
To illustrate the difficulty of making an accurate assessment, the sum of $55,000 was expended on a program which had to be cancelled because of work stoppages, without any salvage values accruing from the expenditures already incurred. On the face of it this represented a production dollar loss of $55,000, but in actual fact the amount which was budgeted for this particular program was substantially greater. The uncompleted program was replaced in the schedule by a program already in inventory which cost much less than the under-expenditure on the originally scheduled program. The result was a loss of a valuable program of high quality, so far as the viewers were concerned, but in terms of the Corporation's expenditures there was a saving in dollars. Subject to the foregoing qualifications, the best calculation which can be made of the dollar value of production losses up to February 29, 1972 is less than 1 per cent of the Corporation's program production budget for the year ($1.2 million out of $151 million) and this in turn was offset in large part by

Has Canada supported the United States in refusing a proposal of the coffee producing countries within the International Coffee Organization for an increase of four cents per pound of coffee to offset the loss occasioned to them by the United States devaluation of the dollar and a further proposal accepted by some of the importing members of the International Coffee Organization to accept two cents per pound increase as a compromise and, if not, what is the Canadian position in respect to these proposed increases in coffee prices?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bruce Howard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Canada did not support the proposals of the coffee producing countries within the International Coffee Organization for adjustments in the price ranges for coffee to offset the devaluation of the U.S. dollar for the following reasons: (a) the ICA price ranges are only trigger points at which export quotas are adjusted and, therefore, are not minimum or maximum prices directly determining producer returns; (b) agreeing to an upward adjustment in the ICA trigger points would have decreased export quotas thus reducing the amount of coffee coming on to the market and creating an artificial shortage of coffee amounting to almost 10 per cent of annual availabilities; (c) the ICA trigger points are set annually taking into account the availability of coffee which, in turn, is reflected in the level of the annual export quota established. At the time of the proposals, already half of the coffee year had passed. In August, the Council of the Coffee Organization will have the opportunity to change the trigger points for the new coffee year taking into account not only any effects of the devaluation of the dollar but also the expected level of trade in coffee for the coming year; (d) Many producing countries immediately devalued their currencies in line with the USA dollar thus offsetting any adverse effects which they might have foreseen for their exports.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary oi State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: HIJACKING-CANADIAN ACTION TO SECURE INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON METHODS OF PREVENTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is a very complicated question. Unless the strike of the airline pilots interferes, we intend to deposit our instrument of ratification of the international convention today. We have also been trying through ICAO to strengthen the enforcement of the conventions that now exist and to which we are party. My colleague, the Minister of Transport, could certainly give an account of the extra measures that have been taken to protect the travelling public against the possibility that hijackers may be aboard or may have some instruments in their baggage. We have taken a number of measures that I hope will be effective, although I have to say what I have said many times before, that I do not think there is any single way or even a combination of ways which could prevent hijackers from operating under certain circumstances.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
That this House regrets the failure of the Government to produce a comprehensive and coherent program to deal with the growing unemployment among our young people and its disregard of youth's legitimate aspirations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion that we have presented to the House today deals with the question of high unemployment among the young people of this country. We are primarily concerned with the high unemployment among young people under the age of 25.
First, I must say that in Canada we have the unfortunate record of having the highest unemployment rate of any industrial country. Naturally, when you have such a high unemployment rate, you are going to have a very, very high unemployment rate in groups such as the young people of this country. The government should be ashamed of this. Indeed, it is not acceptable for Canada to have such a high unemployment rate when this country
3248

June 19, 1972
Unemployment among Youth
has so many resources, technology and educational skills among our people.
When you analyse the employment statistics, you find that the rate of unemployment among the young people of this country under the age of 25 is about twice as high as the unemployment rate among Canadians in general. I suggest that this is a very serious problem. It is something to which we must address ourselves. There are not many excuses which the government or the minister can put forward. We are tired of empty rhetoric. Now is the time for action.
We all realize that there are some problems. We realize that there are a lot of young people hitting the labour market. In spite of that, we must look at the feelings and realities behind the statistics. Over one quarter million young people under the age of 25 in this country are unemployed. No rhetoric in the world can cure this. What we need is action. We need policies to face this very important problem.
At the outset, I wish to read a couple of very short paragraphs from a report that was prepared by the Canadian Council on Social Development as a result of their study of the problems of young people. I quote the last couple of paragraphs. In summary, I believe they set the tone for the debate I am trying to precipitate this afternoon. The Report of the Canadian Council on Social Development reads:
The choice for Canadians is between tinkering with existing programs for the wrong reasons, or embarking on new ventures in policy made imperative by the transitory nature of society and our inability to cope with present difficulties.
This study of youth applying for social assistance illustrates the need for many reforms in the policies, practices, and programs of our social welfare system. But we believe that even more important is recognition by a greater proportion of the general public that the private market economy in its present state cannot by itself provide youth with the opportunities they seek for self-fulfilment, constructive contribution to, and meaningful participation in Canadian society. Acceptance of this premise will demonstrate the need for a comprehensive and integrated approach to policy formulation and implementation encompassing all levels of government and the major social systems-education, manpower, welfare, plus the major institutions of the private market sector.
I think that the approach being used by the Canadian Council on Social Development is one that is on the right track. What we really need are some new approaches and some new values. We cannot rely on the conservative status quo we have been following in the past. Obviously, the approaches we have been taking have been failing. All you have to do to realize this is to look at the statistics. We have many unemployed young people who are totally frustrated and alienated because of the type of system we have in this country. If we look around us, we see that life is rapidly changing each and every day. Technology is far outstriding the change in our social and economic institutions. It is about time that our social and economic institutions caught up with the technological part of our society. We must not just repair the old ship. What we need is a new ship. If we are going to solve this problem that is facing so many Canadians, particularly those under the age of 25, we need a new direction.
According to the latest report from Statistics Canada, the unemployment figures for May are startlingly high. There were 552,000 Canadians unemployed. Of this

number, almost half were under the age of 25. Some 269,000 young people under the age of 25 are unemployed today. This represents 48.7 per cent of the total unemployed in this country. In other words, nearly half the unemployed people in this country are under the age of 25. A large segment of our unemployed is composed of young people between the ages of 14 and 24, but they only make up 26 per cent of the total work force. As you can see, proportionately the rate of unemployment among people is twice as high as it is among Canadians in general. The government must face up to this fact and bring new policies forward in order to cope with the problem.
The rate of unemployment among the young people in this country has been increasing. In May of this year, approximately 13 per cent of young people on the work force between the ages of 14 and 19 were unemployed. Between the ages of 20 and 24, 10.2 per cent of the young people were unemployed. I want to emphasize that these figures do not take into consideration the fact that a lot of the university and high school students are seeking jobs. All you have to do to realize this is to go back to the statistics for the month of January when students were in school. In the month of January this year, 16.6 per cent of the work force between the ages of 14 to 19 were out of work and 11.1 per cent of the work force between the ages of 20 and 24 were out of work. The number of unemployed youth has grown drastically over the past few years.
I wish to refer to one more statistic. In 1966, 6.2 per cent of the young people under the age of 25 were unemployed. The figure for 1972 is 11.5 per cent, thus it has almost doubled in a period of seven years. The situation we are now faced with is indeed serious. In many cases, the young people who are unemployed are just starting a new life, getting married and raising a family. These people do not have jobs. They do not have an adequate income which would enable them to supply good housing, clothing and food for their families. Indeed, this starts off a whole cycle of poverty, financial poverty as well as social and cultural poverty. The children of these families may follow the same route.
Although I do not want to spend too much time on this, the situation facing students in this country is very serious. According to the Department of Manpower, in 1971 there were 1,184,000 students in this country seeking work. Out of that total, there were 212,000 who did not find a job. They could not find a summer job of any sort. Many of those who did, could obtain only temporary or part-time jobs, or else some work which brought them only minimum wages and kept them at a bare subsistance level. As a result, many students were unable to return to university last fall. We find that even those who completed their university education are experiencing difficulty in obtaining employment of the kind they believed they would obtain when they entered university. We found examples of men with Ph.D degrees driving taxis, students with masters degrees working as clerks or secretaries. In the Finance Times of May 29, it was stated that 20 per cent of those who graduated from the University of Toronto this year will not have found jobs by the end of 1972. The article suggests that even this figure may be misleading because half of these students might drop out
June 19, 1972

of the labour market or return to university to continue their studies there. So, the figure might be 40 per cent.
We should remember, too, when we are talking about jobs, whether for students, graduates or young workers, in all too many instances, women are discriminated against. The report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women emphasizes this fact. I should like to urge the government, once again, to take action on the recommendations contained in this report, because there is continuing discrimination against women in many sections of our society solely on account of their sex, without account being taken of their knowledge, experience or ability. It makes me angry to hear the old Elmer Fludds in this Parliament refusing to recognize the fact that women are discriminated against in our work force and in our society generally. I could give hon. members dozens of examples from my own University of Saskatchewan showing how hard it is for women to find jobs. Many of those who do succeed in finding work must take low paid jobs as waitresses or secretaries, receiving only minimum wages. The government must take action to improve this situation as soon as possible; we are already years late in reforming our system.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
The result of the situation I have been describing is this: students are increasingly questioning the validity of the university system. I remember, back in the 'sixties, we were told: If you go to a university you will have a guarantee for life that your income will be higher; you are likely to get a much better job than others; you will find it far easier to raise your family properly. Today, we find this is not true, at least with respect to many of those who are leaving our universities, and old values are being shot down as we find university graduates, those with M.A. or B.A. degrees, failing to find jobs, or finding jobs they could have filled without going to a university at all. As they look across their backyards or alleys they see some of the people who dropped out of school, perhaps holding down a unionized job and making between $10,000 and $12,000 a year while they, with their university education, are not making as much. As I say, many young people are questioning the value of the university system today.
Many universities are becoming increasingly elitist. The Conservative government in Ontario has just increased education fees. This makes the universities more elitist. Most of the students who graduate as lawyers or doctors and business executives come from upper middle-class families. It is almost as though they inherited a medical or legal degree. The chances are that their fathers and mothers were involved in those professions; they had access to a lot of money; they were brought up in the proper milieu when they were going through the school system. Anyone who has studied social psychology knows that young people are influenced by their environment, their families, the books they have in their homes. It is obvious that access to an expensive university system tends to be limited to the sons and daughters of the wealthy. It is they who will enter universities and succeed in finding the better jobs. It is time we got down to grass roots issues and put
Unemployment among Youth
into force policies relevant to the working class people of this country, the young farmers, the average young citizens of Canada. It is time we got away from old policies which are obviously failing, given the fact that half the unemployed are under the age of 25.
Look at some of the answers we have been given by the Liberal government. Many of them have been short term answers. Some have been mere tokenism. Other have been patronizing. Obviously, they have failed. Some have been good.
A few weeks ago the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) introduced amendments to the Manpower Training Act reducing the number of years during which a person had to be in the work force in order to qualify for benefit under the act, from three to one. This is a good move, a step forward. It is a move many of us have been suggesting for years, along with representatives of organizations concerned with young people.
But consider the Opportunities for Youth program. Many of us believed the concept was a good one, one which enabled young people to submit to the department programs in which they were interested, created their own jobs and carry out their own administration. In practice, what has happened has been this: the jobs have gone to the students who do not really need them. That this is the case is apparent from the findings of the Cohen Report. Many of the jobs have gone to the sons and daughters of the upper middle-class. These are the young men and women who are best able to fill in application forms; it is they who have the right contacts and who can afford to gamble because they always have father's bank account to fall back on. As I say, the government realizes this. I am suggesting that hon. gentlemen opposite do something to make sure that jobs created by the Opportunities for Youth program go to those who really need them, not to those who don't.
In this connection, I should also like to mention the travel exchange program and the travel grants. Again, many of these grants go to people who do not really need them; they go to people who would be working or doing something in any case. A press release issued by the Department of the Secretary of State on May 25 announced two travel grants to youth orchestras in Alberta. I have nothing against youth orchestras or the work they may be pursuing, but I question the validity of grants being made in such a direction. In this connection, I quote from the press release.
Grant of $11,375 to the Edmonton youth orchestra for visit, July 22 to August 17, of 100 of its members to Lausanne, Switzerland, for two-week stay, and then travel to Germany and Austria.
The orchestra will, of course, be giving concerts, and it will travel to Germany and Austria. The second grant, of $7,500 has been made to the Calgary youth orchestra; 75 students will take part in a concert tour of England, Germany and Holland from July 2 to August 1. Rather than spend money in this way, it might be better to grant money to people who will be remaining in the country, people who really need it to feed themselves and, perhaps, go on to receive university or post-secondary education at some future date. Despite these programs, not only are more people unemployed and living in a situation of eco-
25319-20J

June 19, 1972
Unemployment among Youth
nomic stress, but increasing numbers are becoming frustrated, adding to the tension we find, especially, in our larger cities. Unless we take some corrective measures soon, we are going to have more and more violence in the years that lie ahead. Obviously, we must search for more solutions.
There are people in the country who tend to give up, who tend simply to go on welfare because they have been unable to find a job, and there is no other choice for them. They find themselves in a system that encourages them not to find work or to have any motivation for finding work. Then again, we have some of the older people in society who like to criticize our young people for being lazy. They criticize their standards, the fact they let their hair grow long or the fact they challenge the norms of present day society. Something must be wrong with a society in which our young people do this, and which forces them into the situation they are facing. I suggest we have to act and to act soon. If we do not, we will have more and more of our young people saying that any value placed by society on institutions is irrelevant, that society must be changed. Perhaps others will declare that they must resort to violence, and this is what I do not want to happen.
Much of this reaction would be prevented if we had programs that provided work for our young people, which gave them something meaningful to pursue in their lives and in the lives of their families. This is why there are a number of suggestions that I want to make. I am repeating suggestions that have been made by this party, by the Canadian Council on Social Development and various other institutions. In talking about unemployment among young people, you cannot divorce it from general unemployment in this country. The important reason there are so many young people unemployed in Canada today is that there is so much general unemployment. The economy is not operating correctly, and I suggest there is no excuse for this. There is no reason for over half a million Canadians being unemployed. No rhetoric or excuse can justify that.
If we are to solve youth unemployment, we will have to start the economy rolling again, and there are a number of ways of doing this. First, we have to solve the problem of foreign ownership. We need more research and development. Many of our graduates go through university but are then unable to find work. Obviously, this research and development is not going to be done if parent plants are not located in Canada. We will have to locate them in Canada if we want to create more jobs in this country.
If I may turn now to something more specific, I should like to detail some of the things that can be done for our young people. I suggest we put more emphasis on on-the-job training so that our young people, regardless of their educational background, receive training on the job. This is very important. Sometimes people have to be retrained three or even four times during their lifetime, especially in a fast-moving technological society. Some of the regulations have to be much more flexible if people are to qualify for training courses of this kind. On-the-job training is relevant today, and is something that should be emphasized a great deal more than it is.

Second, if we are to continue the Opportunity for Youth program, opportunities for youth should be directed more to those who really need those opportunities. Perhaps more importantly, Opportunity for Youth programs or similar programs should be brought in for non-students, for the working class or young farmers, or for those young people who want to start up a business, and so on. Only 9 per cent of the jobs provided through OFY go to non-students. If we continue this program, we must have a similar program for those who are not students.
I also think we will have to have more programs for young people starting farming. In my province and across the country I am told that the average age of farmers is about 57. I think this tells us a great deal about rural Canada. We will have to offer more training for your young rural people, with interest free loans and similar financial help, if we are to provide jobs for our young people in rural Canada.
Then, we will have to do more for young married couples. Many of these young couples are in very severe economic straits and need to be helped. My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has already mentioned that day care centres should be readily available. We should spend more money on day care centres rather than giving gifts, write-offs and tax concessions to the rich corporations of this country. Day care centres provide our young women with an equal opportunity to go out to work or to pursue what they wish to pursue. In addition, there should be more public housing and a greater availability of loans at low interest rates so our young couples can make a better beginning as they enter their working life.
Then, we must have such programs as early retirement for our older people. I do not see why our older people should not have the chance to retire and to draw benefits from security plans, such as the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act at the age of 60. If that were the case, we would open up a whole series of new jobs for our younger people, and it would enable our older people to pursue a more interesting life.
These are some of the things that can be done, so we are making these concrete suggestions today. We will have to do some of these things if we want to find work for a quarter of a million young people who are unemployed today. There is no excuse for this number of unemployed. If we do not do something about it, the situation will snowball; it will worsen and we will then be faced with many more serious social problems. I trust that when the minister speaks he will reply to some of the points that we are going to raise, and will explain to us why the government is not pursuing some of these ideas. Perhaps he will announce new programs that he may have for this quarter of a million young people who are unemployed. They are a very important part of this country and they need jobs as much as anyone else. With that I conclude by once again emphasizing that unemployment is a very serious problem that we cannot overlook, one that will have serious repercussions for the future if we do not act now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I congratulate my colleague to my left for introducing this motion which is a very succinct one, very much to the point, and perhaps one of the most important
June 19, 1972

motions that will be debated in the remaining part of the session.
If I recall correctly from my limited knowledge of history when Alexander the Great was causing great devastation militarily a number of centuries ago, he spared one city because the city fathers indicated to him through an envoy that they were prepared to give him anything in the city with the exception of their young people. Alexander the Great replied that anyone with that kind of attitude, anyone who had that kind of foresight, did not deserve to suffer a military attack. That was the reaction of Alexander the Great.
Today we have "Pierre the Great", the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who has quite a different attitude. If 1 can quote the Prime Minister, who was speaking in London, Ontario on November 11, 1971, he said:
Isn't it true that perhaps more and more people are turning away from the work ethic ... And some of them are unemployed, but their life is more meaningful being unemployed-that's their judgment-than somebody else who works a 40-hour week and produces something which in their judgment is of no use to society and perhaps may even be of negative use-
The Prime Minister is claiming that our young people are turning away from the work ethic, that in fact they rather enjoy being unemployed, that they do not aspire to be creatively employed but are enjoying life just lying around in various parts of the country. As someone has just indicated to me, Pierre the Great should heed the lesson of Alexander the Great. I think the Prime Minister was correct when he said that young people today and people generally would question whether in fact work should be defined as only the creation or production of material wealth. I agree with him in that, but think he is very much out of touch if he still thinks young people in Canada today are satisfied to be on the unemployment roll and wandering across this country in search of jobs. That is certainly not the attitude of the young people I have talked to in the last several months. As a person who has been actively involved with a number of young people across Canada, and as a Member of Parliament talking to those who visit here, I have been very impressed with the attitude of young people as far as future employment is concerned. I suggest that today the greatest significant effort of our young people is the endeavour to find employment. They are as concerned as any age group about becoming productively employed.
One of my colleagues to my left has indicated the statistical problem in some detail. In the last several months I have been accused of emphasizing the statistics of unemployment to a greater extent than I perhaps should, so I will leave that matter as it now is on the record. The hon. member indicated the number of young people in the age group from 14 to 24 who are looking for work, and has also indicated the national average in respect of employment of those under age 24. He has referred to the 30,000 jobs created under the Opportunities for Youth Program, and emphasized the fact that we have spent some $30 million. He indicated that approximately two million Canadians, and the figure 1.8 million is quoted frequently, between the ages of 14 and 25 years are looking for employment.
Unemployment among Youth
What concerns me much more than these statistics and the impact of our economy on these young people, is the fact that from the first day they enter school, that is from kindergarten through the entire educational system, they are urged by their parents, their teachers, their community leaders and their governments to strive to reach that great plateau when they have gained an education and can enter constructive fields. However, there are tens of thousands of young people in this country who have gained university degrees, graduation from technical trade schools and various colleges and high schools, who find themselves frustrated in an unfriendly economy in which they cannot find employment. I think these unemployed young people represent the most serious component of the problem we are discussing today.
I am not going to become involved in a long discussion of this problem, but I could spend a great deal of the next few minutes talking about the magnitude of it and quoting examples of the devastating effect unemployment has on these people. I could quote examples of representations we have received in recent weeks from urban groups, especially those in Toronto, but perhaps I should move on to a discussion of the responsibilities and where they lie, with some elaboration of the suggestion made by my colleague.
We must take first matters first. The fact of the matter is that the problem of unemployment among young people can never be considered totally a government problem. The government should recognize this fact. Regardless of what type of program it adopts, including the Opportunities for Youth program, there is no way this problem can be resolved by purely narrow government involvement. The government must acknowledge the fact that we have to consider the total economy. It must recognize that unless we get industry more actively involved in an effort to create employment for young people we will continue for the next several years with a very heavy degree of unemployment among young people.
In its haste to create a favourable political climate by bragging about the Opportunities for Youth Program, the government has failed to recognize the problem, and has overlooked the importance of getting the economy moving. The government should make more effort to get industry involved. It should provide some kind of incentive to industry to show how worthwhile it is to employ young people. I firmly believe the federal government has never really paid enough attention to the federal-provincial-municipal aspect of this situation. The federal government announced the Opportunities for Youth Program without any consultation whatsoever with the provinces. The province of Ontario, the province of Alberta and other provinces have brought in their own programs and if I can judge by comments made publicly, there was never any great effort to integrate these policies and programs.
I would hasten to add that the federal government is not totally to blame. Certainly, all three levels of government must be brought into play if we are to have a significant impact. The first thing that must be said is that the Opportunities for Youth and the Local Initiatives Programs must undergo very serious re-evaluation. We are talking about 30,000 jobs and about literally hundreds of groups

June 19, 1972
Unemployment among Youth
of young people who have had projects and programs rejected. I suggest they have not fully understood the criteria. Other groups in other communities have had similar projects accepted. The frustration and anxiety caused by this type of activity on the part of the government can in many cases make these programs more destructive than useful.
The fact of the matter is that rural parts of Canada, particularly small communities, have received a great deal less benefit and less opportunity under these government programs. They have less opportunity to become involved in these activities. The hon. member also referred to the lack of opportunity for young people from poor families. It certainly is a fact that very few people from poor families really understand the power structure in order to take advantage of these types of programs. This situation certainly must undergo serious scrutiny.
We must give credit to the minister for his forward looking attitude in respect of manpower programs and for his introduction and passage of the bill which eliminated the three-year requirement of involvement in the labour force. There are many areas of our manpower programs that could be amended to help young people, and one is the 52-week maximum time for upgrading skills. An individual can go to an upgrading school, but after 52 weeks, regardless of whether he has completed his program, he is dumped out. That is one thing that ought to be changed in this type of manpower training program.
We must look as well at the idea of taking these young people from manpower training programs and somehow integrating them into the economy. There is no point in putting people into manpower programs, going through the expense of training them, and then dumping them into an economy in Canada in which there is no opportunity. In many cases, the government has been more interested in taking people off the unemployment rolls than it has been in creating job security. In other words, it has been devising welfare programs. A great deal more effort has to be made to integrate these training programs with the demand for trained workers in our economy. I hope the minister will tell us what he thinks about a five-year program in which industry can be involved in order that when these people complete training programs they can be placed in industry, finding a way from one stage of development to another.
I would say that our educators across the nation, even though education is sometimes thought to be purely a provincial matter, should reassess the type of education they are giving our young people.
I would like every Member of Parliament and every educator in Canada to read a book which has been a bestseller for the past six or seven months. The book is entitled "Future Shock". Perhaps every Member of Parliament has read it. There is a chapter in that book which is devoted to the theme that the educational system is directed more towards producing people geared to many aspects of society in centuries past rather than to people who would fit into the present system. I think everyone should read "Future Shock" to learn the way in which our educational system today produces people, even after 15

or 20 years in the system, who are not really qualified to fit into the society of the 1970's. I would like to say, as a teacher more than as a Member of Parliament, to educators across this country that they must start re-evaluating their educational process so that it will be relevant to the 70's. I submit that what we are providing our young people with today in the way of an education is irrelevant. It is completely out of tune with the 70's, let alone the 80's for which we should be planning. I will debate this with any educator in this country.
I have a couple more points I wish to cram into the 26 minutes allotted to me. My colleague, who speaks for our party in respect of the national health and welfare aspect of the federal government will be touching on this in more detail. However, there must be a re-adjustment of our attitude toward young people so far as welfare is concerned. If I may use the phrase "the adult world" to refer to people beyond age 25, that world refers to young people as being great recipients of welfare. If any one would read the very impressive argument put out by the Canadian Council on Social Development, it would be seen that there is not a preponderance of our young people on welfare. The figure is less than one per cent in the 14-25 year old group compared with in excess of two per cent in the group beyond that age. The fact of the matter is that we must change the attitude we have toward our young people who find themselves in trouble and need a little assistance under our social welfare schemes. If they need assistance they are just as entitled to it as is any adult in Canada.
We should make available to our young people opportunities which would make it possible for them to avoid the necessity of requesting assistance under social welfare programs. More importantly, I would like to see a long serious look taken at the Canada Assistance Plan. At the present moment, no province is entitled to adopt policies which would allow it to replace welfare schemes with work schemes. For example, if the province of Quebec desired to give its young people $100 a month plus a few dollars from its own coffers rather than $50 a month welfare, along with the $50 a month which is available from Ottawa under the cost-sharing agreement, and put them productively to work, that province would not be entitled to do so because under this legislation the provinces which encourage people to work are refused the federal share under the Canada Assistance Plan. In other words, the federal government says that if a province wants to use the payments it receives under the Canada Assistance Plan to put people to work, those payments will be cut off. I believe that is grossly unfair. I think a more liberal attitude could be taken so that provinces which are capable of designing work schemes to productively employ young people would be able to use the federal share of welfare assistance for this purpose.
I have a final comment. I do not wish to dominate the discussion today because I know a dozen of my colleagues on both sides of the House who wish to become involved. In the past several days, I have watched a number of television programs covering various festivals. Last evening everybody saw on national television a program covering the festival held by the "Jesus Freaks". I am not very much aware of the motivation behind these festivals or the psychological motivation behind tens of thousands
June 19, 1972

of young people getting together and worshipping in the way they do, listening to music or getting turned on, or whatever it is. I am not familiar with the psychology behind this, but there are hundreds of thousands of young people who find the energy to get together and enjoy music festivals, religious festivals, or whatever it is.
I wonder whether anyone has seriously considered challenging the young people through federal assistance, to take part in some kind of activity related to their own future. I should like to see some kind of national conference. It could be called a rock conference, a religious conference, an employment conference or something else. Let us have some type of federal encouragement and federal funding which would enable thousands of our young people, not when the problem is right on us but at some appropriate time, to get together and offer their suggestions on what they believe can be done to help alleviate unemployment among young people. I know the Canadian Council on Social Development had a great many of these young people involved in its survey procedures. However, I have never seen a means by which the young people from each province could get together to spend some time in offering suggestions as to ways in which their own future could be assured.
Too frequently politicians like myself and other members, as well as the Minister in charge of youth, whom we never see in this House-what is his name? I forget his name. It is the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), the Opportunities for Youth king. I should have liked to see the Secretary of State here today. I know my colleague on the other side, the outstanding minister, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) will be back in a few minutes to participate. The government is also bringing on another heavyweight, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts). I am very serious about this. I should like to see the federal government challenge the young people from St. John's, Newfoundland, Vancouver or wherever to come to Ottawa and spend a few days talking about their problems. Perhaps they have all kinds of ideas which we have never really tapped.
I remember a few weeks ago a group of young people from Toronto came to my office. They represented a variety of groups which received local initiative grants. They offered numerous suggestions. I must admit, having listened to them for a few minutes or half an hour, I learned a great deal more about the problems of young people than I could learn from Members of Parliament in the next six years. So, why do we not accept this challenge and offer it to our young people. We could tell them we would sponsor a conference of representatives from the universities, schools, councils of all kinds and organizations, to talk about their problems. Perhaps in this way we would receive a little guidance, because I am convinced that if we have to wait for the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State to solve the problem of unemployment among young people we will have to talk about 1980 instead of 1970.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-
Unemployment among Youth ville (Mr. Nystrom) is very serious since it deals with an apparently insoluble problem. In fact, we have been hearing about it for many years, without any solution having ever been found.
The situation in which young people under 25 must live nowadays is neither very nice nor very interesting to observe. We hear people say that today's youth does not want to work anymore and that is why they are in such an unfortunate situation.
Mr. Speaker, today's young people are our children, just as we once were our parents' children, and they are not so different from what we were. They haven't changed, but life styles have however. Twenty-five years ago, it was rather easy to find a job; today, the number of young people being maybe ten times larger, there is a surplus of young manpower in our country. That some young people do not want to work is not new; we always had them. Those who do not want to work do not include only young people 20 or 25 years old. In fact, some people 40, 50 or 55 years old would rather receive welfare allowances than work. They are not so much better than young people 20 or 22 years old.
However, I notice, Mr. Speaker, during my travels across Canada, that our young people are interested in their country, that they want to become part of the Canadian society, if they can, if they are permitted to do so. This is exactly the permission they cannot find.
A while ago, the mover said that 250,000 young people less than 25 years old are unemployed. Yet, these are young people qualified to work and seeking employment. At this time of the year, 1,400,000 students ask permission to work during the summer months in order to continue their studies in the fall, and the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) came up, after the Christmas and New Year's holidays, with the Opportunities for Youth program to offer some help to young students and young unemployed.
These days, we receive from the Department of the Secretary of State-I do not write them, but we receive them-letters stating that 19,000 serious requests were received and that approximately 3,000 were accepted. About 16,000 projects under the Opportunities for Youth programs have been rejected. Perhaps not a single day goes by without a member of Parliament receiving a telephone call from someone in his constituency asking for reconsideration of a project submitted in January, February or March that was refused because it involved spending too much money on purchase of materials, because all the funds and more have been spent, and so on. No request for review can be accepted because the funds have run out. The minister says: We have no more money. But the young people are still there. As indicated by the letters received, these projects are serious and valuable and would help young people. Unfortunately, we do not have the financial means to implement them.
Mr. Speaker, I do not accept to be told that we do not have the financial means to help the young. They represent Canada's future and we have no right to gamble it away. Our duty is to build the future and not to gamble it away.

June 19, 1972
Unemployment among Youth
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions, I said the following: If war was declared tomorrow morning, the 250,000 unemployed under 25 and the 1,400,000 students now looking for summer jobs, that is 1,650,000 young people altogether, would all without exception be enrolled in the armed forces, clothed, fed and housed, and also paid to wage war, to destroy. Anywhere in the world, the necessary funds would be found; the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Secretary of State could not say that there is a shortage of money.
In case of national emergency, we would mobilize all our young people, without exception, to have them wage war, but if we want to develop our country, build something and not destroy, help shape Canada's future, the minister will reply: We have no money. Some citizens play with that. The media find that normal. The minister said there was no money; so there is no money. Why should money be scarce in time of peace and not in time of war? This is miraculous, something that defies comprehension, a real mystery.
Mr. Speaker, it is fortunate that many young people realize today that they have been and are still being deceived.
I remember that during the second world war, when I was 20 or 22 years old, a great many young men did not want to enlist in the army. For 25 years, the Liberal party had boasted that under a Liberal administration, we would never have another war requiring military service. In 1939, when war broke out, the mayor of Montreal was advising young men not to enlist or register. He was locked for five years in a concentration camp. He stayed there five years, not seven days like Pepin, Laberge and Charbonneau who had asked their followers to disregard the law. Today, the situation has changed, but it was very difficult then to get out of prison.
In 1939, young people my age were emerging from an economic crisis that raged from 1929 to 1939. No matter what colleges we graduated from, be it that of Limbour where I studied, or Victoriaville, or Montreal, or even university, and no matter what diplomas stuffed our pockets, there were no jobs available, because of the economic crisis. As soon as war broke out, on September 1, 1939, the then Liberal government, as if by magic, announced suddenly the following day: "Come on; no time to waste. We have found the money. War has just broken out." They were ready, then, to provide us with all our requisites for war.
The same thing is happening today. Of course, we are enjoying peace, but for our young, it is a time of economic crisis even worse than that we have been through, because in 1934-35, we were satisfied with far less than we require today. There is now such a variety of products and entertainments of all sorts available to our young that they are placed in a totally different social environment than the one we had.
Let us take the case of young man or woman of 20 today, who attends university or a CEGEP and holds a job in a plant or office. When the week-end comes, they are still obliged to go to their father and say, "Dad, as I work, could you not lend me $10 or $15 for the week-end?" If the father has five or six other children, if his income is not adequate, they understand. They know what the family
[Mr. Caouette.J
situation is; they do not revolt against the family but against society that keeps them from living decently.
Instead of blaming society for refusing to allow the integration of the young, we call them hearless or ill-mannered. We tend to blame the young generally. In fact, as soon as a small group revolts, we are ready to crush youth as a whole to safeguard the system, the financial system. Nobody denounces financing which is easily available in wartime, but not in peacetime.
Mr. Speaker, we all know-the young people as well as hon. members-that nothing is done in Canada to develop our natural resources. Let us consider the north and everywhere in our provinces. There would be lots of things to do, but since we have no money we remain idle.
I refer particularly to roads, especially Highway 8 between Hull and Montreal whose broadening has been promised for 40 years and which is still being promised for the next election. During an election campaign, numbered stakes are driven in along the highway, making electors believe that the road will be built. The day after the election, the stakes are removed and put away till the next election and the highway remains exactly as it was-

In Ontario it is the same thing.
Today the road is good from the eastern border of Ontario up to Montreal. But on the Ontario side up to Ottawa and where traffic is very heavy there is a small two-lane road hardly allowing two cars to meet. Why not build a four-lane road and recruit young people to do it? We have the same situation internationally. I was in Cameroun for Easter. Mr. Speaker, there I noted that sending technicians to train these people for various jobs is a waste of time because they do not want to learn anything. What they need in these countries is social advisers to make the people aware of their situation. For 100 years we have been spending huge sums to help them. They have not yet understood the reason because their education is not in that direction. Therefore we should be sending them teachers.
In India and in Iran where I went, the same situation prevails. It is not the revolutionnaries who have to be sent there, but social workers who would appeal to the logic of the human being.
In every field in Canada, there are possibilities for helping young people provided the government, no matter which, decides to take the bull by the horns-not by the
June 19, 1972

tail but by the horns-in order to find a solution to the problems of young people, and indirectly help fathers and mothers who would like nothing better than to see their children busy at something for the development of Canada. That would allow them to be themselves and not think of themselves as numbers in a socialist or communist state, or in some group, but as free human beings, able to use their personal resources, to find their whole indentity and to put them at the service of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I was a bit surprised that this motion was put down in the name of the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom) who is, I believe, and who prides himself on being, a progressive socialist. I would not have been surprised if the motion had been put down by one of the fossils from the official opposition, but I do find it surprising that it should stand in the name of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, one of the youngest and most idealistic members of the NDP.
What this motion asks is that the House express regret at what it calls failure to provide a "comprehensive" and "coherent" program. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that those who stand in the way of progress have often been those who said, "You cannot take one step now because you have not drafted the final and complete program." The enemy of the good is often he who pretends to demand the best. Is it the hon. member's prescription that we should not act until we have taped every facet of a problem, until we can bring every weapon in our armoury to bear on its resolution? It seems to me that in his motion the hon. member is lobbying not for a program with action, but for inaction. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it was not surprising to me that, in fact, he did not talk about his motion.
The hon. member did not talk about the need for a comprehensive and coherent program because I suspect that in his heart of hearts he, too, wants us to take practical steps forward whenever we see an area in which we can assist people who have social problems. I doubt that he really wants to insist that we should do nothing until we can do everything, or that we must know everything before we can take any action at all. What the hon. member spent a great deal of the first part of his speech discussing is a serious and grave problem-the extensive unemployment in that sector of the public under the age of 25 years.
This is a problem, a grave problem. It is not a problem that has been generated immediately over the past two or three years. It stems from structural factors in the Canadian economy which result from demographic patterns. Unemployment among the young is part of the general structural difficulties that the Canadian economy faces, not only this year but will face over the coming decade. I would suggest that that challenge is part of the special position of the Canadian economy; because, while our economy provides unique opportunities it also confronts problems that are not found in any other society.
Unemployment among Youth
There is, and the hon. member alluded to it, a problem of high rates of entry into the working force, higher than in any other developed country. There are problems of low levels of productivity, and there are problems of regional disparity, with which the hon. member for Gan-der-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) has been much concerned. There are problems in deciding how we should use our great economic asset, the fact that we are resource rich, in determining a general industrial policy for this country.
The problem of unemployment among the young, which the hon. member has described, is one very important part of the more general question, namely-which is the appropriate industrial policy for Canada to pursue. If one looks back over the past four years of the government's policies, Mr. Speaker, I think one will see that most of them, in the economic area, fit around those four great themes. I have outlined the problems of unemployment, productivity, regional disparity and resource development. No one on this side of the House would suggest that we have dealt with these long term problems perfectly, although we have shown an increasing awareness and understanding of them-I would suggest a much greater understanding of them than any of the opposition parties.
The policy of the New Democratic Party toward developing an industrial policy for Canada is basically the ideal of nationalization. Of course, one is not always sure these days whether it does stand for nationalization. If I understand correctly, the policy of the Waffle group is to press for nationalization but this seems to be resisted by the leadership of the party. It is hard to know which is greater, the dismay of the leadership of the New Democratic Party that some of their followers take these ideals seriously or the disillusiorment of the followers that the leadership of the party does not take them seriously.
The proposals made by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville were rather thin. He suggested that we should expand on-the-job training, seemingly unaware that one of the things the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) has already done has been to increase the grants for manpower training from $20 million to $50 million. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that proportionate to their place in the labour force, youth has a far greater share in manpower programs than do other members of the population. Manpower services are actually heavily tilted in favour of young people who, though forming but 26 per cent of the labour force, claim over 40 per cent of available occupational training places under our Canada Manpower training program. This proportion will likely increase if the eligibility requirements for training and allowances are broadened. Youth seeks the services of Canada manpower centres to an extent far outweighing their relative number. Almost half the people seeking full-time work through Canada manpower centres are under 25. Young workers are among those who are vigorously assisted to find employment and take up new opportunities. In 1970-71, 35 per cent of all those relocated through this program were under 25 years of age.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to stray too far into the field of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who, I understand, will be speaking later in the debate. However,

June 19, 1972
Unemployment among Youth I want to emphasize that, through the provision of career and employment counselling to post-secondary education institutions and through other programs, over 142,000 students were placed in jobs last summer by Canada manpower centres. As I said earlier, on-the-job training grants were increased from $20 million to $50 million and 64 per cent of the people who benefited from these schemes were young people. The hon. member's criticisms of the program, and his suggestions for doing things that we are already doing, brings to mind a line describing a not too successful British politician. It was said that he was "indebted to his memory for his ideas and to his imagination for his facts".
I have not yet discussed the use of the Local Initiatives Program in respect of providing employment for young people, but perhaps before I do that I should say something about the remarks of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PRODUCE PROGRAM TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT AMONG YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
When I was speaking about fossils in the official opposition who might appropriately have proposed the motion proposed by the hon. member for York-ton-Melville, I was not thinking of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate. He is a "progressive" Conservative and should be proud of that fact, as I am sure he is. He did not take the approach that is unfortunately taken by too many members of his party, that the Opportunities for Youth program and the Local Initiatives Program are gifts to our shiftless, lazy youth who are depriving other people of jobs. He did not take that approach and he is right because a Conservative should welcome these programs. I will expand on that later.
He did mention two major factors, however. One was the question of increased incentives for employment. The remarks I have just made about what we are doing under the manpower programs, particularly in respect of the young people, should lead him to conclude that we, as a government, are heading in the right direction. His second suggestion was that there should be a national conference for the young people of this country. As a private member and a backbencher, I would support that suggestion. It has a great deal of merit and should be seriously considered.
What has disappointed me most in the reaction of the first two speakers from the opposition is their failure to give credit where credit is due. In their heart of hearts, both the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville and the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate support the principles which were developed by the government in the Local Initiatives Program and the Opportunities for Youth program. I know it is the duty of the opposition to oppose, but it is not necessarily their duty to oppose everything at all times with all the force at their disposal. Their remarks might have gained more credibility if they had admitted that these are sound imaginative proposals which should be accepted and welcomed.
I said earlier that the Conservatives should support Opportunities for Youth and LIP. If there is one thing that we on the government side hear from the Conservative side it is that big government saps the initiative of citizens and bureaucracy takes away the capacity of the individu-

al to assist with the problems of society. In these two programs, we have not created a large bureaucracy to establish and administer them. We have gone to the people and said, "Let's have your ideas, your enthusiasm, your suggestions, your initiative and we will work with you to assist you and to meet a social need." I suggest that a Conservative, particularly a "progressive" Conservative like the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate, should understand, appreciate and support the concept of a government approach which says, "Let us, with a minimum of bureaucracy and red tape, tap the enthusiasm, the idealism and the initiative of the people who have something to contribute to our society."
It is obvious that the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville should support these programs and principles because they are progressive and pragmatic. Of course, they do not claim to cover all the problems of every individual in society, but with a minimal amount of money enormous numbers of people have been assisted not just to do things for themselves alone but to help other people in the community. I would have applauded the hon. member if he had said that clearly, as I believe it is what is in his heart.
The fact of the matter is that in dealing with this problem of unemployment among young people we have developed programs under LIP and Opportunities for Youth which have been enormously successful and which have not been tried in any other country. Indeed, people from other countries come to see how we administer these programs and to learn our secret. I am not the only one to say that the programs are successful. There was an article in the Toronto Star of June 3, written by Trent Frayne and I would like to quote from it at some length-not that he is more eloquent than I, Mr. Speaker, but because members of the House may be prepared to believe that he is less biased in favour of the government than I. He says:
It was as imaginative an idea for combating high unemployment as anything in western society. It was unique in that, instead of devising winter work projects for the people, the government turned to the people themselves for ideas about the kind of work they wanted to do.
To see how this concept has worked out in practice, I travelled from coast to coast to look at LIP projects. I interviewed dozens of officials and critics, people who got grants and people who received help from projects. My conclusion: The LIP program is a runaway success.
What are the ground rules? A project should be of benefit to the community; it should not compete commercially with established businesses and it should give work to people who need jobs. The point is, though, that the abuses were remarkably few and the criticism soon muted, and what really mattered about the LIP program was that it caught up more than 90,000 people who would otherwise have had no work, permitted them the same freedom of invention and ingenuity that the wealthy enjoy, and directed them towards a new frontier in Canada, social justice for all.

Earlier I referred to the view of some members, in fact many members, of the Conservative party who regard these programs as simply give-aways or contributions to shiftless youth who do not need assistance or help. That is an unfortunate way of looking at these programs. This is not a system by which we give anything away. It is a situation in which the government works with young people to tap their ideas and do things which need to be done at low cost.
What most impresses me about young people in our society is the very strong desire that most of them have to contribute to this society. We all give lip service to the turbulence among young people, their criticism of the society we have, and their opposition to the "system" of the "establishment". I think we should debate more often in the House the problems of concern to young people.
Among young people, there have been two reactions to the society which confronts them, a society which, as we all know, is far from perfect. Some of these young people choose, perhaps through frustration, to opt out. There are people on the drug trip, people who abandon the life of their communities to live in communes, and people who say that our society is so rotten and corrupt that they simply want to amputate themselves from it and hope that they will be uncorrupted by the society in which we live.
There are others, much more numerous and I believe more admirable, who, although disliking many aspects of our society, decide that they will not opt out, but will opt in. They are not pursuing selfish goals for themselves, such as a higher salary, increased security or an easy and soft life. They are young people who feel they have something to contribute in helping their fellowman in this

society. These are the people to whom Opportunities for Youth and the Local Initiatives Program have been directed. It has given them a chance to contribute their energy and ideas to a society which desperately needs their enthusiasm and ideas. These young people are our best hope for the future. If we ignore them, or reject them, it will be to the peril of our society.
Since I have discussed the Local Initiatives Program at some length, I should say a few words about Opportunities for Youth. The programs which we have had under Opportunities for Youth have given the young people in our society an occasion to contribute, something which has been too often neglected in the past. Perhaps I might be pardoned if I make reference to the kinds of things being done in my own area, the constituency of York-Simcoe.
